title: What does it mean when you say an element of a film is "up to the public"?

commenti.body: I believe they really wanna play it safe and be able to please the fans who are into LGBTQ or are LGBTQ themselves but also don't wanna make it so official that it won't bother the people who just don't like their characters being queer and stuff.
I mean the person told me they weren't meant to be LGBT and it isn't written anywhere that they are or are not though
[removed]

I guess maybe they're just saying that there might possibly added text and characterization that could make it capable of being read as queer. Sometimes, we put stuff that has a meaning to it that we don't always intend and maybe that's an acknowledgement of that fact.

whaddya mean by this:

"Or maybe they're just playing it safe by just allowing the viewer to read what they like about it so they better appreciate the work."

I am saying that since the person asking the question  might just believe that about the character, I think it benefits to let them play with the idea that the thing they're asking for might be in some way something official depending on them but allowing others who haven't asked or seen the character in that way to enjoy their own reading about them.
what do you mean official depending on them?
Depending on the person making the LGBT reading on the character.
so a headcanon?

and what do you mean by "play it safe"
like is it possible the character isn't lgbt but they are just refraining from saying it?
Pretty much. They're appealing to the fan of the headcannon because it possibly makes their work look better.

They would like it for some people to be allowed to read them as just a "normal" non-queer character and for others to be able to read them as queer cause it's ambiguity can make it more consumable for everyone.
and ambiguity for example can be if the character's romantic history is never shown or discussed correct?

More broadly I would interpret that statement to mean the following: 


This is ambiguous and so the public can project their own meaning and interpretation of that scene/idea onto the film. I would say that the ending of The Thing, is an example of a film leaving something up to the public as its not clear whether both keith david and kurt russell are parts of the thing.

I think it might be because there might be just a general "vibe" that makes them suspect they might be queer but others will not really think about it that way. You can have a character not be shown to be involved in any romance and people will not think much about it. It just depends in what kind of character you made.
I mean for example if there's a character whose romance is never shown and some people see them as straight or queer then its ambigious?

In my opinion, it should be ambiguous but it is generally the norm to just believe the character is straight and cis unless there is some text hinting to that fact or they show traits that are considered "queer" in some ways.
I mean if it isn't written anywhere by the creators that a character is or isn't queer, then there are no hints and its subjective interpretation correct?

Yeah. I am just saying that as long as there isn't anything hinting to them being queer, they won't be seen as queer (aka straight and cis). We cannot either use a sexuality and being agender in this case because those would be queer and also, even when it is somewhat aknowledged by maybe being pointed that "romance isn't their main interest", I think they will most likely believe that the character is straight but isn't at the moment looking to be with anyone and they will just assume their gender by how they look.

Well I mean in my case;
I asked the person if the character is lgbt and they said its up to the audience and it isn't written anywhere that they are or are not queer then that means the movie does not imply they are queer correct because implied means they are but they just don't say it outright

Yeah and in this case, I think the film doesn't give you an actual reason to see what they are  and in this case, it is just appealing to whoever is watching and allowing them to have their own headcannon so that they feel represented. I mean, potentially the character could be gay or straight but we won't ever really know unless they signal to it.
I think there's a term for this kind of thing in that the work has a certain thing that doesn't exist in it but is added later by the creator as a possibility to appeal to the viewer.

So to end off
if there is character in a movie whose shown no signs of being attracted to anyone we can call their sexuality ambiguous

I think that should be the logical way of reading the character but as of now, we live in a cisheteronormative time where generally characters who have an "unclear" sexual orientation will often be assumed to be non-queer and that they say "it's up to the public" because it helps gain queer and queer-positive followers into their work without having to take the effort of making it queer.
